questions.prompt: Order the rungs of the maturity ladder.
questions.explanation: Ask, collaborate, delegate, automate, build. Put each task on the lowest rung that handles it well.

questions.prompt: Match each need to the feature that captures it.

pairs.left: Access to your apps and data

questions.explanation: Each feature has a job: projects hold knowledge, skills hold procedures, connectors give access, and plugins package workflows.

questions.prompt: What should you have before increasing a workflow's autonomy, for example scheduling it?

options.text: Clear success criteria and consistently good results on real examples
Nothing; automate first and check later

questions.explanation: Define what good means, test on 10–20 real examples, and raise autonomy only once results are consistently good.

questions.prompt: Guardrails should be proportional to a task's ____: light for reversible drafts, strict for irreversible actions.
questions.explanation: Scale guardrails to risk: light review for low risk, approvals and permissions for medium, human decisions for high-stakes or irreversible actions.

questions.prompt: Which belong in a regular maintenance routine? Select all that apply.

options.text: Review memory topics and project files
Re-check facts marked "as of writing" against release notes
Never change a setup once it works

questions.explanation: Claude and your work both change. Review monthly, fix root causes when something goes wrong twice, and stay current with release notes.

questions.prompt: A daily digest silently dropped feedback in other languages for weeks. What would have prevented it?

options.text: Success criteria tested on real samples, plus periodic spot-checks
Running the digest twice a day

questions.explanation: Without a definition of good and a test set, failures stay invisible. Evaluate before automating, and keep spot-checking after.
